chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy. May everyone be free from misery. May no one ever be separated from their happiness. May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such pure lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind teacher, source of all good; O bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just like the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara's pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma's root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara's ocean; O so that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva's ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common paths, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy teachers, O bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
In this meditation we can either offer to the self-generation or we can offer to the Buddha at our heart. We either just visualize or feel Guru-Buddha at our heart. We do a brief self-generation practice.

Then using our powers of imagination, we can offer flowers, incense, lights, perfume, food and music, inner offerings, secret offerings, thatness offerings and more. Just imagine making vast and blissful offerings in this way and that they are received with total delight. If we get distracted, just return back to making offerings either to Guru-Buddha at our heart or to self as the self-generation.

If some bliss arises, then we can use that to meditate on emptiness, understanding it as merely imputed, mere name, not other than emptiness. Then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice. Welcome back all.

shantidevaReading.text:
To maintain this precious mind... Oh, sorry. You guys ready? Now you're ready. Okay.

Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life, Chapter 2: Purifying Negativity

(1) To maintain this precious mind of bodhichitta,
I make excellent offerings to the oceans of good qualities —
The Buddhas, the stainless jewel of the holy Dharma,
And the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

(2) However many flowers and fruits there are,
And all the different types of medicine;
All the jewels there are in the world,
And all the pure, refreshing waters;

(3) Mountains of jewels, forest groves,
And quiet and joyful places;
Heavenly trees adorned with flowers,
And trees whose branches hang with delicious fruits;

(4) Scents that come from the celestial realms,
Incense, wish-granting trees and jewelled trees;
Harvests that need no cultivation,
And all ornaments that are suitable to be offered;

(5) Lakes and pools adorned with lotuses,
And the beautiful call of wild geese;
Everything that is unowned
Throughout all worlds as extensive as space —

(6) Holding these in my mind, I offer them well
To the supreme beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
O Compassionate Ones, holy objects of offering,
Think of me kindly and accept what I offer.

(7) Lacking merit, I am destitute
And have nothing else that I can offer;
Therefore, O Protectors, who think of the welfare of others,
Please accept these for my sake.

(8) Eternally I will offer all my bodies
To the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Out of respect, I will become your servant;
Please accept me, O Supreme Heroes.

(9) Being completely under your care,
I will benefit living beings with no fear of samsara.
I will purify my previous evils
And in future I will commit no more.

(10) Within this sweetly scented bathing chamber
With a clear and glistening crystal floor,
Majestic pillars ablaze with jewels,
And canopies of radiant pearls spread aloft;

(11) With many jewelled vases filled to the brim
With scented waters that steal the mind,
And to the accompaniment of music and song,
I offer ablution to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

(12) I dry their bodies with matchless cloths
That are immaculately clean and scented.
Then I offer to the holy beings
Fragrant garments in magnificent colours.

(13) With various excellent raiments, fine and smooth,
And a multitude of supreme ornaments,
I adorn Arya Samantabhadra,
Manjushri, Avalokiteshvara and all the others.

(14) Just like polishing pure, refined gold,
I anoint the radiant bodies of all the Able Ones
With supreme perfumes whose fragrance pervades
Every part of the three thousand worlds.

(15) To the Able Ones, the supreme objects of offering,
I offer all the beautiful, scented flowers —
Mandaras, upalas, lotuses and so forth —
And exquisite garlands, finely arranged.

(16) I offer them vast and fragrant clouds
Of supreme incense that steal the mind;
And I offer delicacies of the gods,
Together with a variety of food and drink.

(17) I also offer jewelled lamps
Arranged on golden lotuses;
And on polished ground sprinkled with scent
And scattered with beautiful flower petals,

(18) I offer to those with the nature of compassion
A celestial palace resounding with heavenly praise
And hung with beautiful pearls and jewelled ornaments
Whose infinite radiance illuminates space.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
Thanks, Adriana. Welcome back, everyone. So we'll look at some data in a moment.

I am now going to make my data announcement that I have now made. This is the third time. And the requests have not been heeded, totally. So we're on a three-strikes-you're-out policy. So this is the third request. And I ask us all to heed the request, please. So I'm going to repeat it.

So the reason we have this time in the class is to talk about how we're practicing. It's not just random story time. No offense. But it's not just a random story, right? Of an experience or whatever. Because that's not necessarily practical. And sometimes it might not be that helpful for someone to just hear a story from someone. The purpose of the data sharing is to talk about what we're practicing.

So let's say there is a story, like something happened. Maybe something difficult. The data would be like this. This happened. We don't need all the details. We don't need a backstory. We don't need the side plot halfway through. It's like, this happened. This is what I practiced with it. And then this is how it went or didn't go. Like that. So if something happened and there's like a little nice anecdote from life, that's great. But we want to make the main point: this is what I practiced. And it could be, I practiced this and it didn't help at all and I feel miserable still. That's great. That's fine. That's still very useful data. Or it could be, I practiced this and then this happened. But we don't just want the story.

We also, no offense, we don't want magnificent experiences. Right? Like, I walked outside and I saw a Buddha floating down the street, radiating light at me. That's very cool. But there's a commitment that helps us gain realizations in tantra. It's called practicing in secret. And you can read about it in Guide to Dakini Land. And it's actually a cause of swift attainments. There's four special causes of swift attainments and one of those is practicing in secret. So something that happens when you have a special spiritual experience and you just share it openly, like a little willy nilly, you'll find it often fades. And it's a very odd thing and you have to kind of experience it enough times to notice it. And there's reasons we'll discover over time why that's the case.

And often just sharing a random experience even if it's amazing, it doesn't always help other people because they might be going, huh, well that sounds cool for you. I can't even get out of bed in the morning. The Buddhas were flying down the street. And obviously we would love to only have a pure mind when we hear data. But not everyone will. They might just think, huh, now I don't feel particularly inspired. Or huh, you sound a little crazy. Or whatever. Like, huh, doesn't make total sense. And so, I'm just sharing this from experience and having seen the effects of this kind of thing.

So for example, if there was a beautiful experience the best way to share it would be like this. I was practicing XYZ — a certain Dharma practice. And then something really helpful happened where my mind shifted. We don't need the details. The Buddhas zapped down the street and shot lights out of their eyes. And this is my conclusion from that practice. This is why it worked. Ah, that's useful for everyone. But "I just had an amazing experience" — that might not be helpful for everyone. Well, what did you do to get that? What's the practice there? What's the practical conclusion from that?

So I'm not trying to dissuade us from sharing the data. What I'm trying to do is make it so that what we share is useful for us and for everyone. In a way that's really constructive as a group.

Does that make sense? Hopefully no one is discouraged by what I'm saying. You're discouraged by what we're sharing. You have two data points and now you're afraid to talk about them. You don't have to be afraid. All you have to do is share your point and say, this is what I practiced and this is what I learned. So as long as you do that, bingo. You can even say, this is what happened, this is what I practiced and I have no idea what I could learn about it. But we have to include something like that.

And the worst case scenario is that no one listens to me and then we just have this chat in six months again. I've already had the chat twice. That's all that's going to happen. I'm not going to buzz anyone. Dale, you're going to go first.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text:
Two things. This is what happened. I walked out of my apartment. It was a beautiful day. A neighbor had planted these beautiful spring flowers there. And I just stood there and felt the beauty, the happiness in my heart. It wasn't coming from the flowers. It was coming from me. And then I was able to, I think the next day, come outside and say, it's not just for me. I'm giving this to the Buddhas. And that felt even better. So I'm trying to walk around with Buddha in my heart. And when I see something beautiful, I'm giving it to them. So that's the first data point.

Second data point. I don't know if we're talking about this, but you asked us to think about what we desire. So I thought about it, and I don't mean this to be morbid, but for me it's having a good death. And what does that mean for me? That means getting closer in my next life to the Pure Land, maybe starting to study sooner, finding Kadampa Buddhism sooner. But also, mainly, what I can do in this life is increase my merit. And for me, that means giving back and enriching my bodhichitta practice. So those are my two data points.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Perfect. That is an A+. Because you're showing the practice and it's related to what we did last week. Bingo. Well done, Dale. That's perfect. Thank you. Thank you for being brave also. Okay, next. David, then Anne. And then Grady.

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text:
So I enjoyed the steps one and three of the four that you had laid out. Step one was remembering that it's coming from our mind, like a good feeling. Step three is offering it to Buddha at our heart. I found that when I was engaging in some sort of, maybe what would normally be considered an attachment-based activity, perhaps like eating some food or something like that, snacking, if I offered it to the Buddhas, it sort of reduced the amount of clinginess that I experienced with it. So that was very, very nice. So I feel like I had some success with step three.

Step one, I feel like I still have some confusion about. So this is recognizing that the good feeling is coming within my mind. It feels like, to me, it's like a half measure. And so I'm not sure if I'm understanding it correctly. So I'll lay out the way it seems to my mind: say I'm bored at work and there's some stuff I could be doing and I'm not sure, I don't feel that good. And I remember I have some jelly beans in the cabinet. So I go and get the jelly beans, eat those, and it makes my mind feel better. And in that moment I can remember that the good feeling is coming within my mind, but it doesn't feel like a panacea in that moment because I don't have full control over my mind. If I did have full control over my mind, then 100% I wouldn't need the jelly beans.

But from where I'm sitting right now with a mind that's mostly out of control maybe most of the time, it feels like the jelly beans are still serving that purpose. And yeah, I'd like to practice and gain more control over it and this sort of long-term project of getting my mind under control and not needing the jelly beans. But in the meantime, it feels like I still sort of need... I'm playing devil's advocate, but that's the framework that it seems like I'm operating under.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, makes sense. Definitely not a panacea because we have to change our karma and karma is not an instant fix. The main thing with that, again, is that act of offering it to the guru, trying to remember it's coming from the mind, etc. — it's just creating a ton of merit and good fortune in the mind. So the panacea would be like all our problems are solved instantly, but that's not how karma works. We've got to create the karma, we've got to create the cause. So we did create the cause, and over time, the joy of creating that cause will almost be like a panacea because we'll feel so happy about the good causes we created. And then eventually the karma will change and our mind will be completely healed. But yeah, just doing it is perfect.

And we might not feel something instantaneously, right? But that's not the effect of the actions, an instant good feeling. The karma is breaking down our samsara. We do things like that. It's creating the form body of a Buddha. And those effects, they take time to see. Thank you very much.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne
practiceReports.text:
So three weeks ago I started doing Lamrim every day for the first time and I talked a week after that how great that's been. So that went well. And then also maybe I think it was sometime in February we talked about how we really need to do Heart Jewel every day, which is also something I've not ever done. I never did Lamrim. I never did Heart Jewel every day. And then I talked to you and you said instead of doing Heart Jewel every day I could do Buddha Heruka, which I've been doing as much as I could along with Dorje Shugden. So I've been doing that every day along with the Lamrim every day.

And I was interested to hear that those things came first before other meditation practices including TTP. I was very surprised to hear that. And I'm like, okay, I'm going to do the thing. And I could not believe — the things that are happening in my life, it is like everything is going exactly the way I would wish it to. And effortlessly. I'm not trying. It's just falling into my lap and I'm like, wow, it really is true. You can rely completely on the Buddhas and on Dharma and on your Sangha to fulfill all your wishes.

And it's not just that I'm getting everything I want — but I also told you, remember I started writing down all my disturbances, and I was starting off with four or five things a day that were annoying or irritating to me, and I have had day after day after day after day of having no disturbances. And it's not because all of a sudden I've become the most patient lady. It's this practice. It's protection.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah. Fantastic. Yeah, very good. Thank you. Yeah, exactly. So you practiced Heart Jewel and Lamrim. And then, as you said, wishes were fulfilled. Hence the other name for Heart Jewel was Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, right? The more elaborate name. Which is exactly describing what happens, yeah. Yeah, it's Wish-Fulfilling Jewel.

And you did point out — and this is clarified in Modern Buddhism — but yeah, Kadampa Buddhists try to practice Heart Jewel and Lamrim every day, but you can replace the first half of Heart Jewel with the yoga of Buddha Heruka, but then you just still have to include the Dorje Shugden prayers, and then it's the same as doing Heart Jewel. If you check, it's very, very similar. So yeah, I definitely did encourage that, which is very nice.

Grady, yep.

practiceReports.speaker: Grady
practiceReports.text:
Mine might be actually the exact opposite of Anne's. Because I actually really liked Anne's thing that she mentioned a couple weeks ago about writing down her disturbances kind of as they came up and I was like, I'm going to do that. And I did it and I've been doing it. After the first week, I was like, it took me a little bit to get into it and I was like, I think I need to do it a little bit more just to kind of gather the trend a bit. So I've been doing it.

And then last week or whatever, we were moving from that to kind of like when we had good feelings, kind of noting those and defining them. And I found that it was hard to go from the negative to the positive. I was finding the negative disturbances and then there were days where I was like, did I have any good feelings today? It was just like — I had spent two or three weeks doing this, but at the beginning of finding the disturbances, I was like, I didn't really have any disturbances today. And then by the end, I was like, man, I have disturbance after disturbance after disturbance. And then I switched it over and I'm like, I don't think I had any good feelings today. So it's like, I guess that's a lesson in itself of where you're focusing.

But then that was combined with the fact that I also do Heart Jewel and have been extending it further and further in my memorization on Dorje Shugden. So I pretty much do it all in silence and have been memorizing it all as I go, which I find is better for my concentration. And doing the Lamrim is helpful. But I also am combining that with — I don't know if I have very many good feelings. I'm not seeing Buddhas walk down the street. So I guess that's my first data point and it ties into my second one.

And I think I'm just struggling a little bit, but going back to the empowerment where you ask, does what you do matter? I've been having kind of a visceral feeling against that and I've been sitting with that and I feel like the pre-question to that question is: do you want what you do to matter? And that was kind of where I landed on it. And I don't know if I do want — some days I really don't want — I want to find ways that I don't, that every decision doesn't have weight. It's like I don't want the responsibility of like such epic, like, does what I do matter? Almost too much. And it's like every decision is kind of weighty and every decision impacts a ton of people, and at the end of the day I kind of want my decisions to be less weighty and less impactful actually. And so I've been sitting with those things.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, yeah, thanks Grady. That's very useful. So related to watching the mind, this is kind of common — that if we actually watch our mind very closely we can see at first maybe we don't see much, and then we see more and more and more and more. And the thing is, there are delusions functioning all the time as long as we're in samsara. We have, for example, self-grasping functioning every single moment of every single day. Or self-cherishing functioning pretty much every single moment of every day. So from one point of view, if you catch all that you'll have a gigantic list of billions and billions and billions of moments of negativity, and there's all sorts of little non-acceptances and cravings and so on, looking for happiness outside of ourselves.

Right, so from a distance maybe those things are invisible, but if we start to look very very closely we can see a lot of them. That doesn't necessarily mean they weren't there beforehand. That just means we're becoming aware of the delusions that are there anyway. And part of that is just feeling like knowledge is power — like, this is good to know. And not getting overwhelmed by that, but just being really aware of what's going on and really feeling like that's a success in its own right. So that's one thing on that practice.

Second, with respect to what we focus on and the point on the good feelings — what we focus on when we're looking at our mind and we're watching our mind and observing it, we're doing it with a practical aim in mind. So it's not just looking at our mind to look at our mind. We're looking at our mind to practice something. And so Geshe-la one time said: don't ever think about your suffering unless you're using it to train in renunciation and compassion. So this practice of watching our mind — we're not just paying attention to it all, because that kind of attention might become inappropriate attention. Wow, look at all this pain. Huh, there's a lot of pain. There's a lot of worries. Oh, this is really hurting. Like, that might actually be putting a magnifying glass and kind of feeding it a little bit. Right? So the reason we're watching our mind, studying our mind, is to do something practical — to train our mind to let go of the delusions, to change how we think and so on. Or at least to grow our renunciation, our compassion.

So for me, maybe if I was noticing a ton of funny stuff going on inwardly, I just think this is really helping me see that as long as I identify with being an ordinary person I'm just going to be having delusions and pain all the time. And then all of a sudden that experience of seeing all those things going on is very useful. And it will actually give rise to a lot of peace in our heart. Because we'll think, I want to abandon these aggregates. But yeah, the point is, if we don't have a practical outlet of doing that activity, it might not be that useful. And it might end up becoming a little bit unpleasant, actually. So that's the second thing. I just encourage, if you're going to do that practice, just make sure there's an idea of: what am I going to do with this? What's the outlet of this? How can I make this useful for me?

And then third, with respect to mattering — yeah, here, this is a verbiage thing, a usage of the word, right? That sense of weight and heaviness is coming from the self-cherishing mind. So what we're talking about here when we're thinking, do my actions matter — we're trying to really make it clear that it's coming from an altruistic place. So the dependent relationship we looked at in empowerment was this: do other people matter? That was question one. Do other people matter? If yes, then does benefiting them matter? Or working for their benefit matter? And then, if yes, then what I do matters.

So that kind of weight and heaviness that makes it very painful for what we do to matter, where we just want relief, is often coming not because the first two checked off fully. It's coming from the sense of basically, I matter and what I do matters. But that dependent relationship is really, really important. This deep sense — others matter. That's the first domino. And we're just letting that domino kind of organically knock down the other two. Others matter. Their happiness matters. And we're just trying to really let that sink in and be the motivation for getting to the second domino. Therefore, working for their benefit matters. Or basically helping them be free of suffering — that matters. And that's basically compassion and bodhichitta. And then, naturally, that will lead to: what I do each day matters. But it's basically fueled from that other-centered mindset. And then it feels very helpful and inspiring.

I'm just trying to share this because it gives that sense of "what I do matters" but in a very peaceful way. In a very comfortable way. There's other versions of it that are really painful that a lot of people experience. Like people who have a lot of nervousness or fear about performance — like giving a public talk or a speech at work or something like that, or how they do on something risky. They actually have an incredible sense that what they do really matters. But that's not a peaceful mind at all. That's an incredibly painful mind. So the verbiage is the same: what I do matters. But where it's coming from is very different in both instances.

So play around with that a little bit. Like, see, can I get to "what I do matters" but strictly from points one and two. And even maybe just stay with: others matter, others matter, others are important and they matter. And let that naturally flow into "what we do matters." Anyway, those are just a couple ideas. Thanks Grady, much appreciated.

Adriana, yes, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text:
I was having trouble with the four-step practice of generating offerings. I felt like it was a complicated yoga move or something. So I realized I had to break it down a little bit more. And in the first week I just enjoyed looking at things that I liked or that were delicious and I would just say to myself, this is not the source of my happiness. So for some reason that moved my heart more than "my pleasure is coming from within my mind." And it made me remember something that you'd said previously which is the best part of something or someone is their emptiness. Like that's the best part of it. So that was good and a good reminder. If something feels complicated, just make it small. Because it just has to move your heart. So it doesn't matter if it's not the whole thing. That's my takeaway.

And the second thing was — I have a lot of concentration problems in doing Heart Jewel. But then last week you recommended, I think to Kristen, when you're in the first half of the Lamrim meditations to do them right after the refuge prayer. I listened to the recording so I hope I got that right. But for some reason that helped tremendously. It was like a big game changer. And I realized having the Lamrim object kind of at the start of the practice helps you keep focus. And I thought I was a total loser with Heart Jewel. Like I'm the worst. I'm that person who just reads it. I'm thinking about what I'm going to eat for dinner. And I've been trying for many years. And I just thought there's something inherently wrong with me. But for some reason in the last three days I took that advice. So I just feel like, if anybody else feels that way, just don't give up. Just keep trying.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne
practiceReports.text: There's got to be something that shifts the practice.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
That's it. Thanks Adriana. Those are lovely points. So the first one is a very practical idea. If a practice ever seems too complicated or unapproachable in some way, see if you can break it down into a more simple component part. And often there is a more simple component part that we can find. Basically everything that exists is compounded. So you can break down everything into a more simple part. So you're right. "I'm thinking the bliss of this thing is coming from my mind completely" is based on first thinking it is not the real source of my happiness. So it was really nice — you just broke one thing into two. And then focused on the more basic point. And that's just really, really smart. That's really, really nice. It's just a great hack with any problem in life. If it looks too big and complicated, just break it down into more basic parts. Oh, okay. Well, I can do that little bit of it. Oh okay. Now I see some movement.

And then the second practical bit is trying to have a little bit of virtue at the beginning of the practice. Starting off on a good note and then letting it flow from there. Whether it's doing a Lamrim object towards the beginning, or just doing something that makes us feel peaceful and inspired at the beginning, it makes a huge difference. So it's really nice that you can do that. My rule of thumb for that is just have one practice. Every person should have one practice that gets them to a slightly peaceful place at the beginning before they even get going. Or by the time they're done with refuge and bodhichitta they have that one little thing that they do. And you can just do it every time. And then once you get into that nice place, then it's much easier to focus because we feel happy. And when we feel happy with what we're doing, we want to focus on what we're doing. Thank you very much.

I think that's pretty good. Mary Ann, did you have a hand up earlier? Okay. An ephemeral appearance.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Let's take a look at the text. Thank you everyone. A plus. Data sharing for all. I'm very pleased. Thank you for pandering to my wishes.

[Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] So, an offering. Disclosure of Evil. I'm just going to start from the top of it. Unowned offerings. Sorry, the actual offering. Page 62. Unowned offerings. Page 62.

All right, so with all these kinds of offerings and images, etc., the point is: use what's going to move your heart. And what you find absolutely blissful and beautiful. So I did share, I think before, that I talked to one of Geshe-la's most longtime students once. And I asked him what his Pure Land looked like. And he said, a fresh mall. Like a shopping mall. And he's just this older British guy. He's just lived at Manjushri Center for 50 years now. I don't think he does much. So in his mind, the most blissful thing he can imagine is a fresh new shopping mall. And it's just a great teaching. That's what he imagines a Pure Land is like. And it's just showing what's blissful to us is completely dependent on our mind. So please don't feel cordoned in in any way to any of these things.

A lot of us though are a bit dopamine fried. We've been absolutely fried with hits of dopamine. With things that human beings should never have had that many experiences of. Whether it's sounds and sights and so on. It's just too much. So our whole system is out of whack. So also what's beautiful and blissful has gotten a bit miswired for a lot of people. And so the simple pleasures are blissful. But we might need to sit with them a little bit and discover their bliss. Like what's the bliss of a flower? What's the bliss of being offered a flower? What's the bliss of looking at a beautiful jewel? What's the bliss of the play of light? What's the bliss of just sound? Like beautiful sounds. Like up at the temple we have little peepers this time of year that come out. This is the most amazing, beautiful sound. And so maybe we are dopamine fried. And we need certain images, sounds, etc. to view as beautiful. But it is worth, if you just sit there in meditation and you let these offerings come to you and to the Buddhas, and you just imagine the bliss of receiving those offerings — you start to see, ah! These simple pleasures are just so beautiful. And we'll discover it on our own, in our own way.

mainTeaching.speaker: Anne
mainTeaching.text: So is it correct to say that when we're making offerings we can go wild, but when it comes to offering mandalas then we need to stick to a very specific idea of a Pure Land that the Buddhas have revealed to us? This is what it looks like. This is what is in it.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
This is definitely a yes-or-no kind of thing. Generally speaking, we can offer whatever we like in whatever way we like. We want something that is going to be blissful and beautiful and delightful to offer. What the Buddhas have taught is that there are certain things that are incredibly skillful to offer and very wise to offer, and they're crafted in a way that's very beneficial. Hopefully over time we will converge with that view. Offering is just defined as that which delights the Buddhas. That's what an offering is. That which delights the Buddhas. What is that? There are all sorts of little offerings that we can make, but probably the things that we absolutely delight in and feel blissful about in our offering up are probably pretty delightful to the Buddhas too.

One other thing here, trying to make this a little bit more clear: when we make offerings there are three things we want to work on in our mind. Again, don't feel like this is a rulesy thing. This is just what's going to help us get the most out of it.

One, that we're connecting to the merit that's being created. Either through understanding the exact karmic connection of the action we're doing or just generally the merit that's being created.

Two, we want to make the offerings as vast as possible. I was just explaining this a little bit in Heart Jewel. One way that I do it is that I imagine the whole world or the whole room I'm in full of whatever I'm trying to offer. Let's say it's beautiful lamps and lights and crystals and all this stuff, beautiful, amazing lights. I'll imagine the whole room. Then I'll imagine all of Brooklyn — because you have to scale up step by step to make it vast. Your mind's expanding. Now the whole earth, or New York or whatever. You can go at whatever step you like. Now the whole earth is filled with these beautiful lights. Then I imagine the image of the solar system I learned in school. Which I think is probably how it looks. Now that whole thing is filled with amazing lights. I might as well throw in some stars and other beautiful light things in there. Then I'll imagine a whole galaxy. That kind of swirling little disk. That's all filled with light. It's like all of them are being offered to the Buddhas. The point is that you just try to make your mind as vast as possible. Break out of the little box mind that we're in. That's point two.

Point one, remember the merit that's being created. I did ask this on the WhatsApp. No one answered me. I had to lick my wounds for a couple of days. No one answered my question. What makes something meritorious? I think we want to remember basically what is merit. There's two understandings. One means real good fortune — basically the potential to gain spiritual realizations. But there's a more technical thing, which is that it's the main cause of a Buddha's form body. That's what merit is. The main cause of a Buddha's form body. Basically, to get a body of a Buddha. So if we wonder why is making offerings to Buddhas meritorious, this is one reason. That makes a lot of sense. I'm making offerings to the form bodies of Buddhas. What does that do? It creates the cause to get a form body of a Buddha.

Anyway, so then third is to imagine and feel the bliss and delight that the Buddhas are having. The principle of having the delight that we're actually making offerings, that we're actually practicing. But you can just imagine what it would be like for you to delight in one of those wonderful things. And you're actually feeling it. We're actually always feeling it if we think about someone else's delight. Because we're just using our mind to think about their delight. So where's the delight happening? It's in our mind. It's not their delight. It's our delight. We're feeling it. So if you think about the joy of a family member who had some great news recently, and you feel like you think about their joy — if you're feeling their joy, it's your feeling. It's not theirs. It's your mind. So whenever we make offerings, we always want to connect to the sense of the delight and the bliss that's being experienced. And when we do that, we feel it. So these three things will make our offering practice very powerful and just lovely. We just love doing it.

[Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] Among the rare and beautiful items offered up here Shantideva mentions several, such as mountains of jewels and wish-granting trees, that may seem quite unusual to many of us. Where are such mountains of jewels to be found? What is a wish-granting tree and where is it located? To understand all of this, we must first know a little about Buddhist cosmology. The system of viewing the universe is quite different from the one presented by current scientific theory. It contains much that would be difficult to accept if interpreted too literally or concretely. However, if we bear in mind the present purpose of this cosmology — namely that it allows us to see the entire universe as an offering to enlightened ones — the initial strangeness of the system will soon disappear.

Buddha taught that there are countless world systems in the universe. Some are like our own, while others are vastly different. Our own world system is composed of four continents arranged in the cardinal directions. We live in the southern continent. At the center of this world system stands a vast, four-sided mountain. This is Mount Meru. Each side of this mountain has the nature of a different precious substance. The color of the sky over each continent is determined by the light reflected from Mount Meru. Because the southern side of Mount Meru is of the nature of lapis lazuli, which is an incredibly beautiful blue stone, the sky over the southern continent appears blue.

Yeah, of course. What's your explanation? Someone told me something. Oh, okay. Well, I'll go with Buddha.

[Reading:] In a similar fashion, the eastern side of Mount Meru is crystal and reflects a white light towards the eastern continent. The western side is the red of ruby and the northern side is the yellow of gold.

I remember when I first read this, I was so happy. I was just thinking, yeah, I'm going with that. I'm going with Buddha. I was just so happy. Just imagining this. Sitting in my mom's office at our home on the floor, on a pillow, reading this. Just underlining and highlighting everything. It's just incredible.

[Reading:] The minerals and vegetation of each of these continents are different. In addition, each continent possesses a special treasure that is its major attribute. These four treasures, which because of their magnificence are offered to the Buddhas, are a mountain of jewels from the eastern continent, a wish-granting tree from our own southern continent, a wish-granting cow from the western continent, and a harvest of crops that need no cultivation from the northern continent.

We're doing parking at the U.S. Festival as our center job, which we've renamed the Cherishing Committee of Welcoming People. Jeremy suggested that we have code names for everyone, because we get to use walkie-talkies. One person will get to be the wish-granting cow. One person will be a harvest of crops that need no cultivation. You can start vying for your name now, if you'd like. You can put in a request to Jeremy what code name you get.

[Reading:] These gifts, representing all that is most precious and beautiful throughout the universe, together with the sun, the moon, and other special items, can be assembled in an imaginative visualization and presented to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in a form known as a mandala offering. If such a visualized offering is performed seriously, its very vastness and supreme quality can have an extremely positive effect on our mind, and thereby lead to the creation of great merit. A detailed explanation of mandala offerings can be found in the book The New Guide to Dakini Land.

Here, with this practice, we can learn more in both The Great Treasury of Merit and The New Guide to Dakini Land. There are tons of mandala offerings. There are different types of mandala offerings. You can do the outer version. You can do the inner version. You can do the secret and thatness version. You can offer the union of bliss and emptiness as a mandala offering. You can offer your own body, transformed into the mandala itself. There are tons of different applications of this that we can play around with.

The main thing that I want to talk about here is making sure our mind is always absolutely fresh and open. Completely fresh, completely open. Our mind can become very stale. Part of it is because the way the mind works is that it operates through shortcuts. That's how we comprehend things, through shortcuts. At first, we're open-minded about something. Then we learn a bit of it, and then we make a little shortcut in our mind to understand it more simply. When something is new and fresh, we take in all the details. At some point, it becomes a little shortcut in our mind. We can just easily understand it quickly.

When we meet someone new, absolutely brand spanking new — maybe it's on our first date, or a new friend, or someone at a party that we're introduced to, or a family member's new partner — we're experiencing it all as new. We're just taking it in. There's this about them, and there's that about them. We ask some questions, and we start to plug in new info. Then once we know them for a month, very quickly it gets simplified. It's usually like, I like them, or I don't like them. They're this kind of person, or that kind of person. Just some kind of simplification. If we know them for a year, or a decade, or whatever, it's very quick that they become almost like a two-dimensional little icon. Like on a computer, just like a little icon. That's them. All of a sudden, all the nuance and difference disappears. Even though they're different, and they're changing, and there's all this about them, our mind's not taking in all that. Part of it is just survival, and it just makes sense. That's what our mind does. It tries to take complex things and make them simple to understand, just to get around.

The point, though, that we're trying to relate here, is that this habit in our life, if we're not careful, can have an incredibly negative effect. Basically, it makes our whole life feel stale. It makes everything just feel stale. Sometimes I'll eat our old crackers here. They were in an original bag, and then they were in another Ziploc bag. The last step, they end up in a bag with other types of crackers. You know that's really bad — a cracker bag that has six different types of crackers. We have a cookie bag, I think, with that right now. Real freaky stuff. It's just stale. There's something wrong with a really stale cracker. It gives you the willies.

Our life can feel like this. It's because, essentially, we're not seeing things as fresh and new anymore. We're just walking around with some old view. Just a bunch of shortcuts that our mind is just jumping to. Everyone we see, they're that kind of person. I'm that kind of person. Oh, it's just Brooklyn again. One little icon for Brooklyn. All these multifaceted things with tons of nuance and beauty and majesty — just one little icon. This can happen with the Dharma. It's an incredibly painful experience. It's not an obviously painful experience because it just feels that the Dharma has become boring. They're not interesting. It's actually our minds become boring and not interesting. It's very painful because all of a sudden something we loved becomes two-dimensional and stale-seeming.

There's an important skill about clearing the stale gunk from our mind. Like a residue. Largely, it's just about a simple kind of impermanence practice. Most precisely, a subtle impermanence practice. All we have to do is just think: I'm a completely new person doing this for the first time. I've never read this before, and I've never seen this before, and I've never heard this teaching before. Like that. What we're trying to do is see it with the fresh eyes of a beginner, with none of the stale gunk on our mind that's just filling in the gaps with our own biases and preconceived notions and little shortcuts. We're just taking it in all fresh and new, like for the first time. We can even ask the Buddhas, let me see this for the first time, as if I know nothing, as if I've never heard this teaching before, I've never heard about the mandala before. And I was just like a child at Buddha's feet, and he's explaining to us about the mandala. What would it be like to have that kind of openness and freshness of mind?

So in reality, this is actually true, right? This is factual. We are seeing it for the first time. It's just our mind that's backfilling it, saying, yeah, yeah, I know this, seen this, read this. But in reality, we're a completely new person in every single moment, completely fresh in every moment, like a beginner in every moment. It's just our mind that's going, yeah, yeah, same old me, doing the same old thing.

Sometimes what I'll do is just a little physical motion, just to ground it. I'm not saying this is like an official Dharma teaching, but just a little silly thing that I'll do. I'll just imagine all my little mental grooves like lines in sand. I'll just go like this, like that, and just blow them all fresh. Just imagine all the little grooves in my mind. They're like this. They're like that. Why did they do this? Why did they do that? I'm like this. I'm like that. I like this. I don't like that. Just like that. Like an Etch A Sketch or something. Those little things where you can draw on the sand. You can shake it up, right? It all just gets fresh again.

We can do this every day. We can especially do this with the Dharma. It basically is just remembering subtle impermanence. We're just thinking, I'm new. I'm fresh. I'm a brand new person in every moment. When we have that openness of mind, when we come to the teachings, we'll see so much beauty. We'll be amazed, basically, by what we see.

I was thinking of Milo at our White Tara empowerment. Some of you know this story, but I explained in the empowerment when we had it here that she has seven eyes that represent the seven types of wisdom. He was, I think, laying underneath a seat. Grady would probably remember better, or Kristen. He was kind of laying underneath a seat in the back. It went on for a while. Then he just was like, seven eyes! I think that's basically what he did. It really hit him. We're just like, yeah, seven eyes. Maybe it's just a metaphor. But it hit him. Seven eyes! Whoa! I sometimes will remember that. Yeah, let me have that same mind with everything I read in the Dharma. Mount Meru. Mount Meru. Right on one side because of the ruby that's on the mountain.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Or, wow, happiness comes from inner peace. Or, wow, the self is just merely imputed. Or, wow, I can correctly identify myself as Heruka, Vajrayogini, or some other guru deity, just through labeling. Anyway, I'm just sharing this because as we go through these teachings we're going to keep seeing things that we kind of know to some degree, that we've learned at different times. But as scholars and students, we always want to make sure we're wiping the old crust from our eyes. We're seeing them as completely fresh teachings and really letting them come in.

This is going to be really helpful for us as teachers — as training teachers or actual teachers — because we'll start seeing the teachings in the way the students see the teachings. And that will help us really help them. And we'll come into a class with that freshness and vigor of having discovered it for the first time. And people will love that. They'll find it contagious and beautiful.

Ryan, you have a hand there?

mainTeaching.speaker: Ryan
mainTeaching.text: Thank you for bringing this up. Because that's the exact experience I had today. So I want to understand the subtle impermanence, I get it intellectually, but how do I actually make it work for me to move me to the point that I want to listen to the teachings? So this morning at the GP class that happened, you explained karma one-on-one to a five-year-old, because there were a lot of newcomers there. And I was sitting in the back, restless. I'm like, I get the causes and effects. I heard quite a few teachings recently. And like, okay, get to the point, Kyle. Get to the point. Where are we going with that? What is this? Do actions matter? Get to the point. But you were like really 15 minutes on the causes and effects explaining that. And I was really restless and bored in a way. So yeah, how can I get these fresh eyes? And I usually love when you go over a teaching because with my memory loss, with my forgetfulness, I can refresh my mind. But with this teaching, somehow I was like...

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah, yeah. We don't have a ton of time on this right now because we need to take a break. But what I'll say to you, Ryan, is that with this exact specific experience — like "yeah, yeah, heard this, blah, blah, blah" — the key thing that we want to think instantaneously is: this means I do not understand this topic. So whenever there's boredom, that means I do not understand it. All caps. And if we just start training ourself, like a little hook, every time. We go, oh, hmm, cause and effect, karma. The second that yawn comes in, just think: that means I don't understand it. Great! Good, I'm hearing something I don't understand at all. Okay, this is a time for me to understand it. Or to figure out what I don't understand. And now we'll start looking at it in a fresh way.

The trick that our mind is doing, right, is we're going, I do understand it. And what we're doing there is we're slapping on some old shortcut that we've developed in our mind. "This means that." Which isn't really the meaning. And that's all we're hearing. We're hearing our old shortcut that's not actually what's going on. And that's boring. But it's not because karma is boring, or any teaching is boring — it's because the shortcut we've chosen to try to understand it is boring. And overly simplistic.

Whenever we understand a teaching, we can't help but get more and more and more of it. We just can't wait until another person talks about it, or brings it up again, because we have this living, vibrant experience of it that's getting watered by them talking about it. Even if they know nothing about it. We're just like, yes! We're talking about that again. Offerings, karma, emptiness, whatever. I was just thinking about that. I feel so blessed about this topic. Yeah, you keep talking about it.

If it's stale, it just means our mind is stale. And that just means we don't understand it. So that's what I would encourage you to do in that moment. That's not as much on subtle impermanence, but that's just the best tool with this exact problem. It's just to always instantaneously think, I don't get this topic at all. Oh, cool. I'm a total beginner then. Because I'm bored by it. That's what I would suggest.

So let's take a breather until 6:15. Announcement-wise: Anne's teaching on karma next Saturday, so Ryan, we know what you're doing — 11 to 2, Saturday, on karma. Very good. And then Living in the Present, I'll be doing on the 18th. And then we have our Vajradaka burning offering that night. Purification by fire. And we have a new grill to burn in. Lime green, baby. A lime green grill. So it's going to get wild here. So join in the fun.

It's our karma quarter. We did it in the Sunday class too, and we did it in the Saturday morning class this week also. So lots of karma — and this whole chapter is on karma. So we've got lots of it going on. So we better freshen up our little stale minds if we've got them. And bring some childlike wonder to this topic.

Oh, Mary Ann, you had a hand there?

mainTeaching.speaker: Mary Ann
mainTeaching.text: Can you at some point explain prerequisites for the burning ceremony?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Prerequisites for the burning ceremony? None. Just interest. We're just doing the puja, so you don't need any prerequisites. We just think about something we want to purify, and we chuck it in the fire. Like that.

Okay, let's just do a brief dedication. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications. Okay, thank you.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.
chantedPrayers.note: Only the Liberating Prayer portion of Session 2 prayers was captured in the transcript.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
All right, welcome back, everyone. Hope you're all alive-ish. Alive physically, but dead on the inside. We can have Brooklyn shirts. Let's say that and sell them. It would be very nice. KMC Brooklyn.

Yeah, so we kind of ended with this idea of trying to have a fresh mind. There's a couple of little things you can do. I mean, thinking about subtle impermanence really is the solution to the problem. So we can improve our experience of that. Within that, sometimes it just — like what I do sometimes — I just feel like, if I was an alien showing up in this world for the first time, what would that be like? I've never seen Earth before. I've never seen humans before. I've never seen Brooklyn before. I've never seen Buddhas before. I've just showed up on this Earth. It would just be like every little thing. We wouldn't even know the texture of anything that we saw. We have no idea. Is the carpet squishy? Or is it hard? Or would it cut you? What does this food taste like? We would just be in a completely open mind. That's the point. Again, it's just like a little hack or something to kind of try to get in that same place. What would it be like to have no concept even of how anything worked or who anyone was? What would it be like to be in that open of a place?

Alternatively, we can improve our practice of exchanging self with others. This does the job pretty well too. We just think: how does so-and-so see this place? Just get into their world. It's incredibly delightful. I remember once I was in a Dharma class where we were having a lot of the formal group discussions. It was getting a little bit boring for me. I told the senior practitioner. She said, all I do is I just keep thinking, why are they asking that question? Like from inside them, why are they asking that question? Then I just feel amazed and I have this sense of wonder because I'm in this completely different point of view. It was very helpful. She was very kindly helping me see, oh, this is your mind that's bored because you're being boring. If you don't want to be boring, just exchange self with others. See what it's like to look at the world from their point of view. Whoa — whole new view, whole new perspective, completely different. This is also a very useful practice. We just ask, how does so-and-so see this teaching? How does so-and-so look at this situation or this problem? Like that. It helps to have someone at least around who has some kind of an open mind, so you're not just exchanging self with bored views. But there's people out there who have that. Some adults, a lot of children, some other people, some quirky people, a lot of Buddhists — so we can at least use our Sangha. Anyway, this is also a helpful way to just get into this fresh mindset, a very beautiful and fresh perspective.

Lastly, we can just think: how do the Buddhas see this? And they see everything as new every moment. It's one of their qualities that's explained in Ocean of Nectar. How do the Buddhas see this? And then if we get into their point of view, yeah, it's very alive and fascinating and incredible. Anyway, there's just some more ideas on the same kind of vein.

All right, so let's take a look at the text. Oh, yeah, Ryan, yeah?

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: I want to come back to something you talked about — offerings — and you threw in a word to find the delight in the offerings. Can you make that practical, like step one, step two, step three? For me, when I do water offerings, I have absolutely no delight. Like I would do it with no delight. But if I would help out in the kitchen here or help out volunteering, okay, I can find the delight because I see that. Yeah, but whatever, like, I don't get no delight. So how do you connect?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Why do you get delight helping out here?

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: Because I see — because I want every person to feel, to have the potential of refuge and find healing, like I got healing. But I don't see that with the water offerings.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Why does that bring you delight, wishing those people that?

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: Because I got healing here, and I found this place for refuge, and I want everyone in Brooklyn to have that potential. But water offerings — yes, if you ask me to do it, I'll do it. It's going to work against my miserliness. But to say "delight, connecting" — yeah, can you make that connect practical, not here, here?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: The reason you delight in assisting, etc., is that you see the benefits of it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
So that's all you have to do. See the benefits in making water offerings, and then you'll find delight in it. What are the benefits? Check out Joyful Path to Good Fortune. Go to the index, water offerings, and then report back what you find.

I'll try to send over a transcript from Geshe-la. This is incredible, what he said about making 100 water bowls. You're not having fun doing seven — what we try to do is 100 every day. And he was explaining that we should do them every day at temples, and so on, and we should do them four times a day actually, so everyone gets a chance to do them. And he said, when you see the benefits of them, people will basically be fighting over the opportunity. Like, oh, I want to sign up first to do the 100 water bowls, which takes like 40 minutes or so to do.

Right. So the question is, do I understand the benefits? The benefits are very clearly explained in Joyful Path to Good Fortune. So I would suggest checking that out and thinking about them a little bit. And that would make us delight. Thank you. Good question.

Okay. Now, page 65. [Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] Making offerings to the Three Jewels — Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha — is predominantly an activity of the mind. Actual material gifts are not required. And so even the poorest person, provided their motivation is pure and their visualization expansive, can make the most magnificent offerings. This practice is designed to overcome the narrowness of our miserly attitudes. And its benefits can be vast indeed.

Okay. So just related to Ryan's point there about miserliness, this is something that would definitely bring us delight in offering: fully understanding the pain of miserliness and the joy of becoming free of it. The joy of freedom from miserliness.

And so we were talking last class about desires and what we want and what we kind of crave. And one of the things that makes that so painful — it's not liking things that makes it painful, it's craving them. Feeling that we need them and that we don't want to part from them. That's what makes it so painful. If we could just think, that's nice, I'll take it or leave it — there's no pain. That's nice, ooh, I'll take it and I'll leave it. That's fine. Well that's nice, I met that nice person. Oh, they died. Okay. Take it, leave it. Oh, I met that nice friend. Oh, they don't like me anymore. Take it, leave it. Like that. Just like pick it up, drop it. No kind of sunk cost fallacy in our mind. Not like, "but I invested in that, I needed that" — just like, oh, that's nice.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
There's no problem, right? Miserliness, attachment, and craving makes liking things incredibly painful. It makes the thing that makes life bearable — which are beautiful experiences — incredibly painful and misery-inducing. So it's very useful, right, to just start to see this. What does the pain of miserliness look like for me? What does the pain of craving look like for me? And we want to try to really associate those words with pain.

Because the hard thing about dealing with attachment, unlike anger, is because there's a pleasure component to it. From one point of view, it's easier to deal with anger, right? Because anger is painful, obviously. There's just no pleasure anywhere. With attachment, there's a little bit of pleasure and then a lot of pain. But that little bit of pleasure makes it much harder to deal with. And often we're willing to put in the effort for that little bit of pleasure.

So what we need to do is to really try to see: what's the pain of miserliness? What's the pain of craving? And start to see that's the hard part. That's the difficult part. And then once we start meditating on that and thinking about that, we'll think anything I can do to overcome these minds actually feels urgent. It feels urgent to be able to overcome these minds because they're so painful. Not urgent in a deluded way, in an impatient way, but urgent in a driven way, a focused way. I don't want to keep this pain of miserliness. I don't want to keep this pain of craving anymore. I'm done with it.

Once we get the insight, we love giving things away because it tears at our miserliness every time we give away. Especially our time. People in Western culture are very attached to time. Not everyone is, but at least in America we're attached to time. Time, time, time. Even worse than Europeans and so on. Americans are particularly bad, especially New Yorkers. Schedule. Time. What's the time? What's the time? What time does that start? You're late. You're late. We're just obsessed with this conception. It's just imputation, right? Like everything else. Time. It's just a name, right? Time. Time. Just a word. There's no time there, right? We're obsessed defending time, guarding our time. We're attached to something. It's just a name.

So you just start giving it away. Oh, it stings if we're attached to it. Keeping our time for what we want to do, right, stings. We can start thinking, this is great, I'm breaking down my miserliness. Oh yeah, every time we give away, it starts to break it down. It's eroding it. It's destroying the miserliness. As long as we're doing it for that purpose. If we're doing it out of guilt, out of pressure, then it's not decreasing the delusions, obviously. But if we do it with this exact intention — I'm doing it to destroy my miserliness and my attachment — then it breaks it down.

Same with giving things, like money, things that we like, and so on. Even just as simple as, we're out to eat, we're sharing a pizza with someone, there's one slice left. We know they really want that slice. And we did the math, and technically it's our slice. And we're like — you, you get that slice. It's like we're running onto Normandy. You know, that's the kind of bravery it takes us. Charging into battle. We feel like such a heroic bodhisattva in that moment. Oh, that melted cheese and sauce. It's basically worth a dollar.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Look at that. It's very fun to just do this. And we're just breaking down our miserliness. It's so helpful. It's just like little things in life that we're doing, right? These little acts of giving.

So the point here, just to make it clear, is that making offerings is going to help us do it. But we need to really see the pain of miserliness and craving for this to be appealing to us. And we want to have a sense of drive, like, I really want to do it. And of course, we can start to break it down in these little ways in life, just practicing giving — the perfection of giving. But then when we practice offerings, it'll start to really break it down too. This will also feed our delight in making offerings.

It breaks down our self-grasping a lot too, because the self-grasping mind imputes a little barrier around this lump of cells, right? It's just an imputed barrier, right? There's no barrier. We're just all cells in one body of life. We're one. So there's no real barrier, right? It's just the self-grasping mind that hallucinates a barrier of an independent self. So every time we practice giving, making offerings and so on, we're breaking down this conception. We're transgressing against it.

It's like back in the day when there was the nuclear war protests or nuclear proliferation protests. There was a line, right? And if you crossed the line, they'd arrest you. And they would have a line, and people would just go to cross the line and go get arrested. And it was like a transgressive act, right? Like, we're just showing you, your line doesn't scare us. It's like a strong action. It's like saying we're not backing down or whatever. I don't know anything about those protests or who is right and wrong, so I'm not saying one side or the other. I'm just saying this idea of going over the line. So when we give, when we make offerings, we're going over the line. We're breaking down the line of self and other, self and Buddhas, whatever. We're seeing no line. I'm not buying into this hallucinated boundary that my mind has made. Anyway, so this is also like this idea of — we're eroding something here.

[Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] The story is told of a small child who wished very much to be able to offer something precious to the Buddha of his day. Since he was poor and could afford nothing, he filled the bowl with dust and held it aloft, visualizing it as resplendent with gold. The strength and purity of his motivation were so powerful that he accumulated vast merit. He was later reborn as the great Buddhist king and benefactor, Ashoka. During his reign, he did much to establish the Dharma in India and Sri Lanka. One day alone, he caused one million religious monuments to be built, some of which can still be seen today.

[Reading:] If we recognize the enlightened beings as having overcome all obstacles and possessing all good qualities, our practice of making offerings to them will bring us closer to their supreme attainment.

So just think about that sentence. Why? Recognizing that enlightened beings have overcome all obstacles and possess all good qualities — why is the act of recognizing that making our offerings to them bring us closer to their supreme attainment? Why is that important? Anyone have a hunch, idea?

David, yeah? I'm doing it with faith. Yeah, some admiring faith, wishing faith, etc. Yeah, I think that's a facet. Anyone else have a thought? Can we get the mic? Yeah, sorry. Mixing our minds? Oh, sorry, we need to turn it on. I think it's not on yet.

teaching.speaker: Mary Ann
teaching.text: Just mixing our minds with the Buddha's mind? Just taking the boundary down?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. Yeah, that's a nice way to say it, Mary Ann. Thank you. Yes, it's related to faith, but it's a nice elucidation.

So, from one point of view, are we recognizing enlightened beings if we're not recognizing that they've overcome all obstacles and possess all good qualities? That's not an enlightened being that hasn't done that. What is that? That's not an enlightened being. That's, again, a simplification in our mind, like a little 2D icon that our mind has made. It's not like a living Buddha. So we're not going to come closer to enlightenment in the same way, just relating to this 2D thing. It's still helping us, but it's not in the same power.

Ultimately, we have to work backwards with these kind of things. Ultimately, what's enlightenment? It's thinking, basically, I'm a Buddha, not other than emptiness. Or I'm Heruka, Vajrayogini, Buddha Shakyamuni, not other than emptiness. That's enlightenment. And so that's the real truth. When we see that, we're seeing the real truth, finally. This is the actual truth. So we want to be able to see that.

So yeah, we do things like the practice of generation stage and completion stage, which quite directly help us do that. But then, what helps us do those practices? Well, meditating on emptiness helps us do those practices because we stop grasping at the self. But also the practice of bodhichitta and exchanging self with others, because we learn how to impute our I on a Buddha's body and mind and stop cherishing an ordinary self, so that we can identify ourselves as a Buddha instead of a suffering living being. And what helps us do that? Our practice of renunciation, because it makes us see that it's just the nature of suffering to identify with an ordinary being. But what helps us do that is actually thinking enlightenment is possible at all. Because you can't develop renunciation without thinking liberation and enlightenment are possible. That's one of the Four Noble Truths. Because your mind won't be motivated to think about suffering if there's not an alternative. The Fourth Noble Truth is believing in true cessations. Basically, liberation is possible. That's the feeling of the Fourth Noble Truth. Enlightenment is possible. Liberation is possible. It's only when we think of that, right, that we're actually motivated to think about suffering. If it's just suffering, then we just have to look on the bright side of samsara and try to make it okay. If there's liberation and enlightenment, then we're motivated to think about suffering. Because we think, great, that's going to help me stop identifying with the suffering being and identify as a Buddha.

So we can say then, we've moved all the way backwards through all the stages of the path to basically just basic refuge and thinking, there are Buddhas. And I'm relating to the enlightened world. It's only when we start making a relationship with the enlightened world that we're going to want to develop renunciation, that we're going to develop bodhichitta, that we're going to be able to realize emptiness, that we're going to label I on our body and mind as Heruka or Vajrayogini or any other guru deity. So anyway, I'm just trying to explain this because this is just showing why this first step of the practice of refuge — like seeing Buddha images, starting to relate to them, starting to relate to enlightenment at all — it's helping us make a relationship with the truth, the actual truth, and see past the ordinariness of life. And it's only through doing that that then the rest of the stages of the path follow. We have to have some relationship to enlightened beings or enlightenment itself. First it seems separate, and then one day it will seem who we are.

So yeah, when we're making offerings, we're trying to upgrade our understanding of enlightenment and enlightened beings every time. And this is going to make this connection. We're going to start to see we're not separate from that.

Okay. [Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] Such an attainment depends upon gaining successive realizations along the path. And to gain these realizations, we need a great wealth of merit or positive energy. The disciples who lived at the time of Buddha Shakyamuni had great stores of such positive merit. And just by hearing one word of Buddha's teachings, some of them quickly attained realizations. The first turning of the wheel of Dharma, for instance, when Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths, several disciples gained a direct realization of emptiness, the highest reality. And some even attained the state of nirvana, complete personal liberation from all suffering. The Dharma taught these days is the same as that taught by Buddha Shakyamuni. And those who teach it are just like Buddha himself. So why is it that even though we listen to teachings for months at a time, we do not attain realizations? It is simply due to our lack of accumulated merit. Therefore, if we wish to gain realizations, we must gather a great wealth of merit. And one of the main methods of doing this is to make offerings to the Enlightened Ones.

[Reading:] The benefit of making such offerings has been supported by the experience of many meditators in the past. There's an account of a fully ordained nun who received a vision of Avalokiteshvara, the Buddha of Compassion, as a direct result of making mandala offerings.

Bhikshuni Palmo. She's the Nyungne lineage holder, basically. We like her a lot. When you do Nyungne practice, which is on the 14th and 15th of April for Buddha's Enlightenment Day, when you make prostrations, you imagine she's on your crown, making prostrations with you. And she just has a lot of energy. She just keeps going. So she's a special lineage guru of ours.

[Reading:] The great spiritual guide, Je Tsongkhapa, used the practice of making mandala offerings to gain a direct realization of emptiness. In fact, this practice is recommended by the teachers of all Mahayana Buddhist traditions.

So practically, we just want to start offering the things that we crave and desire, and that we want, and that we're miserly of. We want to start doing that a lot, if we don't already. Give it away. Give it away. It doesn't have to be a physical giving, because over time, we'll see everything is just imputed. So there's no difference between handing someone a dollar and imputing in our mind that we're handing someone a dollar. What's the difference? It's just imputed. They're both imputed. One, we kind of know it's imputed. And the other, we think is real. That's the only difference. We just think it's real. It's just imputed there. So it's all in the imagination.

So we just sit there. We take whatever we crave or desire that we're clinging on to. It can be objects of the senses — forms, tastes, smells, sounds, objects of touch, and so on. It can be inner things or more ethereal things like praise, reputation, status, and so on. It can be certain people, certain experiences, whatever. And we just imagine offering them up, giving them away, and trying to get to the sense of: I freely give it away.

Let's say we're attached to money. It is uncanny how much this will work if you just do it. So you just imagine — it's nice to put it in a mandala because it has everything in there, but you can do it without a mandala involved. So you just sit there, and you put as much wealth as you could possibly imagine in there. Don't offer dirty little dollar bills. Don't do that. But anything that represents wealth and beauty — pearls and jewels, gold, good stuff, stuff that people actually like. Just imagine so much of it, like a mind-boggling amount. And then just imagine giving it to the Buddhas and that they receive it with delight. Thinking, I'm overcoming my attachment to this.

If we do it over and over, we will be shocked that our craving just stops with money, for example. And we'll think, that was the easiest thing I've ever done. That was the most no-brainer thing. It was so easy. I was fighting my craving, my attachment. I was battling it for all this time. All I needed to do, which is to keep imagining offering it over and over and over again. That's all I needed to do.

And every time we're beset with some kind of craving, in that moment, same thing. We offer it up. We just imagine making huge offerings of whatever that thing is, in a nice purified form.
