So if it's a person, try not to offer their nasty little rotting body. Because Buddhas don't really want that. It's kind of gross. It smells. What does Geshe-la say? It looks toad-like and stunted, the human body. But offer their Buddha body to the Buddhas. Infinite versions of their Buddha-enlightened body. And offer that up. And if we just do that over and over again, the attachment will break down to that person. Just keep giving it away.

Of course, when we get a chance, physically do it. Because we grasp, we believe that it's high stakes when we physically do something. So it can often feel more impactful because it feels high stakes. Because we're doing it mentally, it doesn't feel high stakes. So yeah, when we can do it physically, that's great too. But it is very nice to start to really feed our little giving protocol in our mind, our offerings protocol in our mind. So it gets very strong.

Adriana, yeah.

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text: Okay. I have a question on the relationship between purification and offering. Because this is new to me — that this is really framed, I guess framing this as a purification practice and like a real obstacle that we have for realization is not having merit. And I'm wondering, I want to make sure I'm not like, oh, cool, I can just ease up on the Vajrasattva practice and just do offerings instead. Do you have a way that you combine them? How do you think of them in relationship to each other?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. I got your question, yeah. So the relationship between purification and something like making offerings, which is associated usually with accumulating merit. We kind of want to keep them in those boxes. They're not heavy boxes. When we practice purification, we're accumulating merit. When we're practicing offerings, we're purifying. So they're not rigid boxes. They are useful categories, though, because they're slightly different emphasis.

When we talk about purification, we're thinking about breaking down the obstacles to liberation and enlightenment. And then when we're talking about accumulating merit, it's more about growing the qualities of the enlightened mind. It's a slightly different feeling. So accumulation of merit is like adding. And then purification is like subtracting. So it's a slightly different feeling, and there's a slightly different function, actually.

Yeah. So I wouldn't stop doing the Vajrasattva practice. But it's just nice to play around with and get a nice connection to the power of making offerings and how multifaceted this one singular practice is. It has a lot of different functions.

In the oral instructions of Mahamudra teachings, Geshe-la said, what is a pure mind? And he just said, it's correct imagination. That's what a pure mind is. Which is like just seeing an enlightened world with your imagination. And so if that's what purification is trying to help you do, that's great. But we can see the practice of making offerings is helping us develop that too. It's not like in its own little box. It's separate.

So anyway, yeah, that's just a thought. Yeah, thanks, Adriana. Round four? Round three? Round four for Ryan? That's great. You're hungry for the Dharma.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: That means I do not understand.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: So, you were talking about miserliness and craving. So let's say if I crave validation, which is painful too. How can I use this offering — like your example — to get rid of that? Like, for example, you said with miserliness. Okay, let's say if I crave — I have miserliness with time. Okay, if I offer the time, I will hopefully... How can I use craving for validation, which is so destructive, to use this offering thing to get rid of it? Not to purify, but to really get rid of that craving.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. So how would we apply it to one of the worldly concerns? Especially things like wishing for validation, which is essentially attaching to reputation or praise. How do we do that when the craving arises? How can we bring a feeling of offerings into that?

Step one with this specific thing: I would just imagine I'm in the presence of Buddha. And Buddha loves me and accepts me perfectly as I am. And just loves me so much. And I would feel that love. Okay? That's step one. And that will help a lot already with the validation. Because often the reason we want validation is because we don't feel loved and valued. But there's already people who know everything — Buddhas — and they love us. Completely. So we should feel that love. And let that love be felt.

Then, if we wanted to go further, we could just ask, like, what can I offer that kind of represents the validation that I'm seeking? Is it about connection that I'm seeking? Is it about self-worth? Is it actual words of praise? Just come up with something. It doesn't matter that much. And then we just imagine that as an offering that we're giving away to the Buddhas. And usually with something insubstantial like validation, it's good to make it a 3D object. This is one of these things where you just have to see it, and then it works. But it's just making it a 3D object that you offer that represents it, makes it more powerful.

So Geshe-la explains this in The Great Treasury of Merit, in the practice on offering our spiritual practice. We offer all of our realizations in the form of a little island with all these beautiful treasures and stuff on it. And we imagine offering these incredible islands of treasures. And they're representing our spiritual realizations that we want to develop. So you just make it a 3D object that somehow relates to it in some way. So if it's like, okay, I'm craving connection, you just think, what represents connection for me? What would be a beautiful thing that would represent connection? Like, maybe it would be an incredible tropical forest in the Philippines. It's all interconnected and beautiful and linked, and it's all symbiotic and supporting each other, and the water that goes in here is creating the tree that goes there, and that feeds this creature. It's this incredible embodiment of connection that you're offering. If it's something about self-worth, we would come up with some sort of 3D object that represented that. It could even be something simple, like a beautiful trophy or something that we're offering, that represents praise and approval or something.

You get the idea, yeah? So then you just imagine offering it, and then you just imagine the Buddhas are delighted, the mind of great bliss, receiving the offering. And just, again, it's one of those things where you're just like, how is that going to help my validation craving? And it just does, like clockwork. Yeah, it's fantastic. Yeah, so thanks for asking.

Okay, we're going to wrap up in a second. Let's all work on this throughout the week. You get the practice, the idea, yeah? So we're just taking things that we crave, desire, etc., and we're offering them up, or giving them. It could be mental, it could be physical. We're trying to break down that barrier of self-grasping, miserliness, craving that we put around ourselves, trying to transgress against it. And this is a very practical activity. This is something we're actively doing throughout the day. Yeah, it'll be a good week. Okay, I think that's it. Thank you all.

Let's have some time for discussion now. Let's have Anne and Dale, and Anne P and Ryan, and Mary Ann, David, and Jose. Thank you.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Two, one, yay! Yay, our little box people are back. I think the practice is pretty obvious. Any addendums? Offer stuff? Remember three tips while offering stuff. Yes, thank you.

All right, let's do it. We'll just dedicate here. We can think of the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. You can make any other personal dedications or prayers. Okay, thank you. Happy offering, everyone.
